extracted.intended_audience: young printers, tradesmen, and civic-minded colonists
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and behavioral maxims for printers, partners, and civic organizers in 18th‑century colonial towns — covering business partnerships, press ethics, club organization, public projects, and local defense. Primarily advice on how to run a printing business and participate in public institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refuse infamous printing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Young printers should refuse to 'pollute their presses' by printing infamous or improper matter even if profitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin cautions that printers must steadily refuse corrupt jobs; he notes by his example that such refusal will not, on the whole, injure one's interests. Intended as an ethical and reputational standard for printers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear partnership accounting terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When entering partnerships (e.g., supplying a press and types to a partner), explicitly state profit shares and expense responsibilities and require regular accounts and remittances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin's Carolina partnership specified he would receive one-third of profits and pay one-third of expenses; lack of clear accounting by his partner caused problems. Clear written terms and regular accounting are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft explicit partnership articles to avoid disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Set out in writing every duty and expectation for each partner to prevent later jealousy, breach of friendship, lawsuits, or other disagreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin attributes the amicable ending of his partnerships to having very explicitly settled everything in articles; he recommends this precaution to all entering partnerships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train and promote workmen via limited-term supported establishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish printing-houses for competent journeymen on terms that enable them, after a term (e.g., six years), to purchase types and continue independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin used this model to promote trustworthy workmen; most succeeded and several families were raised by this practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate young women in practical accounts/bookkeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend teaching young females bookkeeping/accounting (rather than primarily music or dancing) to equip them for widowhood or managing a mercantile house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin praises a widow in Charleston who managed accounts with regularity and eventually purchased the printing-house; he argues account knowledge is more useful in common life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the safer medical choice when risks symmetric (inoculation example)
rubrics_metrics.description: When faced with medical decisions where regret is likely either way, choose the safer option (Franklin regrets not inoculating his son and thus recommends the safer course).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin notes parental regret may be equal in either outcome, so parents should choose the safer intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep small deliberative clubs limited and secret
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a convenient small number (e.g., twelve) and secrecy for a club (the Junto) to avoid improper applicants and preserve usefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin explains the Junto's secrecy and size were intentional to avoid admitting unsuitable persons; when growth was desired, form subordinate clubs instead of enlarging the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use subordinate clubs to scale influence without enlarging core group
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of enlarging a successful club, have each member form a subordinate club with the same rules and report back to the main club.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: more young citizens improved, better sense of public sentiment, promotion of business interests by wider recommendations, and spreading the Junto's sentiments through several clubs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have club members propose queries and report proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize clubs with structured queries for discussion and require subordinate clubs to report what passed back to the main body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedure was used to inform the Junto and to influence public opinion on particular occasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform public services by proposing practical, equitable measures (city watch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify abuses in public arrangements (e.g., constables' six-shilling excusal fee) and propose practical reforms such as hiring professional watchmen and levying taxes proportionate to property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin wrote to his club about the inequality of the excusal fee and proposed hiring proper men and proportionate taxation; preparing public minds in clubs paved the way for later laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote organized fire prevention and mutual aid
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish cautions about carelessness leading to fires, propose a company for ready extinguishing and mutual assistance, and require members to maintain equipment and meet monthly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin's Union Fire Company obliged members to keep leather buckets, strong bags, baskets, and meet monthly to discuss fire response; small fines bought equipment. The institution greatly reduced losses from fire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Govern fire companies with rules on proposals and expenditures
rubrics_metrics.description: No money should be disposed of until the meeting following the proposal; use fines for equipment purchase; require attendance or levy fines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural rule (delay till next meeting) and financial governance ensured deliberation and proper use of funds in the fire company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow reasonable delay before votes to permit opponents to attend
rubrics_metrics.description: When a vote is to be taken that may be controversial, grant a short delay (e.g., an hour) to allow opposing members to arrive so the vote is fair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin recounts letting an hour pass before voting on laying out stock in lottery tickets; the delay was agreed fair but resulted in no opposing members showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use printed pamphlets and organized instruments to mobilize voluntary defense
rubrics_metrics.description: To form voluntary military association: write a pamphlet to expose the danger, propose an association instrument, distribute printed copies, provide pens and ink at meetings, read and explain the instrument, and collect signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin's Plain Truth pamphlet prepared minds; at a meeting he read the draft, explained it, distributed copies, and collected over twelve hundred hands, ultimately mobilizing ten thousand subscribers who armed and trained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize regiments by volunteer choice and elected officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary companies should choose their own officers and meet regularly to be instructed in discipline and manual exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associators formed companies and regiments, chose officers, met weekly for instruction, and had women provide colors by subscription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use personal courtesy to build political or business goodwill
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate relationships by requesting to borrow and returning a scarce book with a warm note of thanks to create goodwill with influential persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin recounts borrowing a gentleman's rare book and returning it with an appreciative note, after which the gentleman became friendly and ready to serve him—illustrating prudent removal of enmity by civility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vest public buildings in trustees for use by any persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: When building a public meeting house, vest both house and ground in trustees explicitly for use by any preacher of any persuasion, to avoid sectarian exclusivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin describes a large building in Philadelphia intended for any preacher or persuasion; trusteeship prevented the building from serving only one sect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider logistics and resources when advising charitable projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Advise that charitable projects (e.g., orphan houses) be located and executed where resources and workmen are available rather than transporting materials or people at great expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin declined to contribute to Whitefield's plan to build in Georgia because of local shortages and recommended building where materials and workmen existed (suggesting bringing children to the house instead).

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of language instruction: start with modern tongues
rubrics_metrics.description: Argues it may be more effective to begin language education with modern languages (French, Italian, Spanish) before Latin, because modern tongues are useful and may ease later Latin study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin notes that learning French/Italian/Spanish helped him later with Latin, and proposes reconsidering the common mode of beginning with Latin first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid publishing everything you preach if you value lasting popular influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing sermons and writings opens preachers to written criticism ('litera scripta manet') which can reduce their influence; itinerant preachers may benefit from repeated oral delivery rather than written records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin observes Whitefield's writing gave critics material to attack, diminishing his sect's growth; repeated oral performance improves delivery and pleases audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act with principle regarding offices: don't solicit, refuse, or resign lightly
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a rule of never asking for an office, never refusing one when offered, and not resigning an office voluntarily to preserve political leverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin recounts his rule (with a small addition) about offices — he would not ask, refuse, or resign — which he used to retain his clerkship and political standing.
